pedagogy.summary:
- **Age:** 8–11 years

- **Topic:** Comparing Possible Solutions

- **Standards — UK (DfE Design & Technology KS2, Evaluate):** pupils "evaluate their ideas and products against their own design criteria and consider the views of others to improve their work," building on generating and communicating a range of ideas.

- **Standards — US (NGSS 3-5-ETS1-2):** "[curriculum wording omitted; reference 3-5-ETS1-2, 4-ESS3-2, MS-ETS1-2]."

- **Operational details:** Given a defined problem (criteria + constraints already set), the child generates AT LEAST THREE distinct candidate solutions, then compares them systematically against the same criteria and constraints rather than picking a favourite on impulse. The core skill is holding one shared yardstick across options: rating each solution on each criterion, checking each against each constraint, and then SELECTING the most promising one WITH REASONING that refers back to the evidence — not 'I like it' but 'B meets the leak and budget criteria that A fails.' Teach that comparison needs the same criteria applied to every option, and that the best solution is often a trade-off, not a winner on every row.
bestPractices: Require genuinely MULTIPLE ideas (≥3) before any judging — use a quick divergent phase so children don't anchor on their first idea.
Compare all options on the SAME criteria: a shared matrix (solutions × criteria) forces apples-to-apples rather than each idea judged on its own terms.
Separate criteria (rate how well) from constraints (pass/fail must-meet): a solution that breaks a constraint is out regardless of how well it scores elsewhere.
Demand reasoning tied to the matrix: the child must justify the pick by pointing at the rows, naming the trade-off accepted.
Normalise trade-offs — show a case where no option wins every row, so 'most promising overall' becomes the honest goal, not perfection.
keyRepresentations: Decision/comparison matrix: solutions as rows, criteria as columns, a rating in each cell, with a separate constraint pass/fail gate.
Constraint gate: a red flag that eliminates any solution breaching a materials/time/cost limit before scoring.
Side-by-side solution cards, each carrying its ratings, for at-a-glance comparison.
A 'because…' reasoning slot that must reference specific matrix cells to justify the selection.
commonMisconceptions: Picking the first or best-liked idea instead of comparing several against the criteria.
Judging each solution on different, self-chosen strengths rather than one shared set of criteria.
Ignoring constraints — choosing a solution that scores well but breaks the budget or materials limit.
Believing the best solution must win on every criterion, rather than being the best overall trade-off.
Selecting without reasoning, or with reasoning ('it looks cool') unconnected to the criteria and evidence.

learn.summary: Children aged 8–11 learn to compare multiple possible design solutions against one shared set of criteria and constraints, then select the most promising with reasoning that points at the evidence. The core skill is holding a single yardstick across at least three distinct options: rating each on each criterion, gating out any that break a must-meet constraint, and accepting that the best choice is often a trade-off rather than a winner on every row. Activities span building a working comparison matrix, defending a choice in dialogue, reading a worked matrix, and judging pre-filled comparisons — each targeting a different part of generate-compare-select.

activities.title: Solution Showdown: build and reason across your own comparison matrix
feedback: If the learner enters one design plus minor variants, ask for three genuinely different approaches (for example, different materials, structures or ways of reducing heat transfer) before any judging; praise divergence first, evaluation second.
If a chosen solution breaches a material, size, or cost limit, flag it at the constraint gate and have the child re-check each candidate pass/fail before comparing on performance.

If the justification never mentions the stated criteria, point back to the grid: 'Which keeps the ice coldest? Which fits? Which is under budget?' and require the 'because…' to tag the specific cells.

OPTIONAL interaction examples that make the mechanism concrete: a live tally that re-highlights the current 'most promising' as ratings change; a red flag that drops out a constraint-breaker the instant a limit is flipped; dragging the winning card into a 'because…' slot that must reference cells. These are illustrative, not required.
activities.rationale: Systematic comparison is a procedure the child must enact, so building and reasoning across a matrix of their own options exercises generating, comparing on shared criteria, constraint-gating, and justifying — the full target skill rather than recognition of someone else's comparison.
sourceClaims: KS2 pupils generate, develop and communicate a range of ideas and evaluate their ideas and products against their own design criteria, considering the views of others to improve their work.
learnerActions: Start from a defined brief whose criteria and constraints are already set (e.g. a lunchbox insulator that keeps an ice cube frozen from morning to lunch, fits the box, uses only allowed materials, and stays under budget).
Invent at least three genuinely different candidate solutions and lay them out as side-by-side cards before judging any of them.
Rate each solution on every criterion by filling the cells of a shared solutions×criteria grid.
Apply a constraint gate: mark each solution pass/fail on each must-meet limit (materials, size, time, cost); any solution that breaks a constraint is eliminated regardless of its ratings.
Select the most promising solution and justify it by pointing at specific grid cells — e.g. 'B keeps the ice frozen longer and stays under budget where A fails' — naming the trade-off accepted.
Work through at least one case engineered so no option wins every row, so 'most promising overall' becomes the honest goal.
activities.intendedInsight: A defensible choice emerges from one yardstick applied to every option; a constraint is a gate that eliminates, not a preference to weigh, and the best solution is usually an explicit trade-off you can point to.

activities.title: Defend your choice to a design mentor
feedback: Keep redirecting any preference- or looks-based answer back to a named criterion until the child reasons across all three options.

Treat an answer to a changed-condition question (budget, time) that explains how the changed criterion or constraint would or would not change the ranking as a sign the child is reasoning from criteria; confidence alone is not evidence, because a child can confidently defend a favourite.
activities.rationale: Spoken, responsive questioning rehearses the justification habit and can surface fixation or preference-based picks. It reinforces reasoning-from-criteria but does not by itself provide the structured matrix, so it complements rather than replaces the building activity.
sourceClaims: KS2 pupils generate, develop and communicate a range of ideas and evaluate their ideas and products against their own design criteria, considering the views of others to improve their work.
learnerActions: Present three candidate solutions and an initial pick to a mentor (teacher, peer, or in-role character) who will not accept 'I like it' or 'it looks cool'.
Answer pressing questions that force reasoning across all three ideas: 'Compared to your other two ideas, why this one?' and 'Which criterion does each idea win or lose on?'

Respond to follow-ups that test the robustness of the choice: 'Which of the other two came closest, and what ruled it out?', 'If the budget doubled, would you still choose this?', 'If it had to stay frozen until home time, would your choice change?'
activities.intendedInsight: A choice is only justified when it is argued against the alternatives on the shared criteria and constraints; impulse picks collapse under 'which criterion does it win on?'

activities.title: Read a worked comparison matrix
feedback: Prompt the child to predict a cell's rating before revealing it, then check their reasoning against the annotation.
After revealing the winner, ask the child which row the winner loses on, to make the trade-off explicit.
activities.rationale: A pre-authored worked example gives clear exposition of what a thorough comparison and an honest trade-off look like. It demonstrates the structure but does not make the child generate options or apply the yardstick themselves, so it is best used as a model before independent building.
learnerActions: Study an annotated decision matrix comparing several solutions across the same criteria.
Reveal, cell by cell, why each solution rates as it does on each criterion.
Reveal the reasoning behind the chosen winner, including where the trade-off lies and which rows it loses.
activities.intendedInsight: A good comparison applies the same criteria to every option and names the trade-off behind the winner; this is what a defensible selection looks like before you build your own.

activities.title: Judge pre-filled comparisons
feedback: If a learner selects a constraint-breaker, point out that a failed must-meet gate eliminates an option regardless of how well it scores on other rows.
If a justification cites preference rather than rows, require it to name the specific criteria the chosen solution wins and the trade-off it accepts.
activities.rationale: Reading a pre-filled matrix and drawing the conclusion can assess the evaluative judgement. Note that it hands the child a completed matrix rather than having them build and reason across their own, so it checks the comparison and selection judgement but does not elicit the generation and construction parts of the skill.
learnerActions: Given a completed solutions×criteria matrix, choose the most promising solution and state why in terms of the rows.
Sort candidate options into 'meets constraints' and 'eliminated' categories.
Rank the solutions that remain after setting aside any that fail a must-meet constraint by overall fit against the criteria.
Complete a 'chosen because…' justification that references specific rows of the matrix.
activities.intendedInsight: Drawing the right conclusion from a comparison means reading across shared criteria, gating constraint-breakers first, and tying the choice to named rows.

constraints: Require at least three genuinely distinct solutions before any judging; a quick divergent phase helps children avoid anchoring on their first idea (design fixation).
Compare all options on the SAME criteria — a shared matrix forces apples-to-apples rather than each idea judged on its own strengths.
Separate criteria (rate how well) from constraints (pass/fail must-meet): a solution that breaks a constraint is eliminated regardless of how well it scores elsewhere.
Demand reasoning tied to the matrix: the child justifies the pick by pointing at rows and naming the trade-off accepted, not 'I like it'.
Normalise trade-offs by including a case where no option wins every row, so 'most promising overall' becomes the goal rather than perfection.

The read-a-worked-matrix and judge-pre-filled activities are scaffolds for the evaluative judgement; they demonstrate or assess comparison but do not make the child generate options or apply one yardstick to their own ideas, which is the target skill.
Dialogue practice reinforces justification but does not supply the structured matrix or constraint-gating; use it alongside, not instead of, a building activity.
The misconception that the best solution must win on every criterion should be directly addressed by the rigged no-clear-winner case, so the child experiences an honest trade-off.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; the two cited sources (NGSS 3-5-ETS1-2 and DfE D&T KS2) were not re-fetched and both carry verified:false in the source row. All activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

The source framed a 2D interactive matrix as 'ideal' and a 3D environment as 'poor' on catalog-fit grounds; these rankings have been converted into complementary activities with stated affordances/limits rather than universal claims about which medium can teach the skill. No 'adds nothing' or 'only this teaches' claim is asserted; the 3D entry's narrow point (it adds manipulation the comparison task does not need) is noted as a limit, not a law.

The diagnostic lunchbox-insulator example assumes 'traps the most air so it insulates best' — generally true for still air, but real insulation performance depends on materials and setup; treat it as a plausible illustrative claim, not a guaranteed outcome, and it is not stated in any learner-facing activity.

The NGSS 'generate and compare' claim cited for 'Judge pre-filled comparisons' supports only the comparison/selection half of the principle; that activity does not exercise generation, so the claim is partial, topic-adjacent support rather than full coverage.

The original generic 'B meets the leak and budget criteria that A fails' example has been adapted to the lunchbox brief's actual criteria so the worked example stays internally coherent; the underlying contrast (evidence-based reasoning vs preference) is preserved.
The source links a constraint-gate reteach to prerequisite mt_Z5-fSCOBep; internal IDs have been removed from learner-facing guidance as instructed.

probeDeeper: You picked this one — which of the other two came closest, and what made you rule it out?
If the budget were doubled, would you still choose the same design? Why?
Suppose it had to keep the ice frozen until home time, not just lunch — would your choice change?
assess.correctAnswer: The child generates three genuinely different solutions, weighs each explicitly against the stated criteria (keeps ice frozen, fits the box) and constraints (allowed materials, budget), and selects one with reasons that refer back to those criteria and constraints — e.g. 'this one traps the most air so it insulates best and still fits, and it's under budget'.

errorPatterns.pattern: Fixates on the first idea and elaborates it instead of generating real alternatives (design fixation) — 'I'll just make this one better'.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Require three visibly different starting shapes before any judging; praise divergence first, evaluation second.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Produces one design plus minor variants of it, not three distinct approaches; resists sketching a genuinely different option.

errorPatterns.pattern: Compares on personal preference or looks rather than against the stated criteria and constraints ('I like this one, it's cooler').
errorPatterns.nextMove: Point back to the criteria card: 'Which keeps the ice coldest? Which fits? Which is under budget?' Make the comparison run through each criterion.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Justification never mentions keeping the ice frozen, fitting the box, materials, or budget.

errorPatterns.pattern: Ignores the constraints — selects a design that won't fit, uses banned materials, or busts the budget.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Have the child check each candidate against the constraints as a pass/fail gate before comparing on performance; reconnect to how the problem was defined.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Chosen design violates a material, size, or cost limit and the child doesn't notice.

responseLevels.gap: Offers one idea (or near-copies of it); chooses on preference; disregards criteria or constraints.
responseLevels.full: Generates three distinct solutions, evaluates each against every criterion and constraint, and selects one with reasoning that ties the choice back to how well it meets the defined problem — and can defend it against the runner-up.
responseLevels.partial: Generates two or three options but compares them loosely — checks some criteria, or names constraints without systematically applying them, so the choice is only partly justified.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Here is the problem: design a lunchbox insulator that keeps an ice cube frozen from morning until lunch. It must fit inside this lunchbox, use only the materials on the table, and cost no more than the budget on the card. Come up with three different possible designs, then decide which one you'd build — talk me through why as you go. (Set the task, provide the materials/criteria/constraint card, and watch what the child does; do not explain how to compare.)
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: Watching, not asking, reveals whether the child truly compares: a child who understands generates several options and holds them against the criteria, while a child who doesn't fixates on the first idea and defends it, or picks on looks. You can only see the comparison behaviour — which options were considered and rejected and why — by observing the process, not by asking 'how do you compare designs?'

sources.claim: KS2 pupils generate, develop and communicate a range of ideas and evaluate their ideas and products against their own design criteria, considering the views of others to improve their work.
sources.source: DfE National Curriculum: Design & Technology programmes of study, KS2 (Design & Evaluate)
